mcqs.question: What is a Terraform module, conceptually?
options: A special resource type only cloud providers can define
A file format only used for storing state
A synonym for a Terraform provider
A reusable directory of Terraform config with defined inputs and outputs, similar to a function
mcqs.explanation: A module packages reusable infrastructure logic behind explicit inputs (variables) and outputs, the same idea as a function — call it with different inputs to get differently-configured infrastructure without duplicating the underlying resource logic. It's unrelated to providers or state file format.

mcqs.question: Why do most teams prefer separate state files (or directories) per environment over Terraform workspaces for dev/stage/prod?
options: Separate state provides stronger physical isolation, reducing the risk of accidentally applying against the wrong environment
Workspaces aren't supported for production infrastructure
Workspaces can only be used with a single provider
Separate state files require no backend configuration at all
mcqs.explanation: Workspaces share the same backend and code path, switched by a command — a typo or forgotten `workspace select` can mean applying against the wrong environment. Fully separate state (and often separate configs) makes that mistake structurally harder, which is why higher-stakes environments usually favor it. Workspaces work with any provider and both approaches need a backend.

mcqs.question: What's the main risk of putting dev, staging, and prod resources in one giant root module?
options: Terraform doesn't allow more than one environment per root module
Every apply's blast radius spans all environments at once, and it's easy to accidentally plan/apply against the wrong one
It makes the HCL syntax invalid
It prevents you from using any modules at all
mcqs.explanation: The technical risk is entirely about blast radius and accident-proofing: one shared state and one shared apply means a mistake isn't contained to a single environment. Terraform has no syntactic restriction against this structure — the problem is operational, not technical, and modules remain usable regardless.

mcqs.question: A shared module used by five teams needs a breaking change -- renaming a required input variable. What's the correct way to ship it?
options: Rename the variable in place and let every consumer pick it up on their next `terraform init`
Bump the module's major version and let each consuming team upgrade to it deliberately, on their own schedule
Avoid ever making breaking changes to shared modules under any circumstances
Delete the old module and create an entirely new one with a different name
mcqs.explanation: Shared modules should follow the same semver discipline as any dependency: a breaking change is a major version bump that consumers opt into, not something that silently lands on everyone's next init. Refusing all breaking changes forever isn't realistic, and renaming the whole module avoids the versioning problem without solving it.

mcqs.question: A team notices tracing a single misconfigured security group rule requires following a variable through four nested modules, none of which add logic beyond passing the value along. What does this indicate?
options: The team needs to add even more modules to further organize the code
This is expected and healthy Terraform structure regardless of module depth
The nesting has become indirection without real abstraction -- a module that just forwards a resource's own arguments 1:1 isn't earning its complexity and should be inlined
The problem is unrelated to module structure and is purely a state-file issue
mcqs.explanation: A module should encapsulate a real decision or genuinely reusable unit; one that only forwards arguments with no added logic or defaults adds debugging cost without abstraction value. Adding more modules would make this worse, not better, and the root cause here is structural, not state-related.
